::: {.notes}
*⏱ 0:45 · Tanya*

*[Check with Jadey: farmers directly, or extension / TA staff on their behalf? The FOR card assumes the latter.]*

**Tanya:** This is where I come in as Nestlé. I'm IndieVisual. It's a one-person shop, so when I say IndieVisual built something, I mean I did.

Jadey had a published package. What it didn't have was a way for someone with no R install and no command line to get a report. So I built Dirt Data Reports: a Shiny app that sits on top of `{soils}`, takes a CSV and a few choices, and hands back a finished Quarto report.

No R. No terminal. Zero friction. Here's what it looks like.

**[next slide: the recorded demo]**

::: {.notes}
*⏱ 1:30–2:00 · Tanya, narrating over the recording*

**[press space or click the video to play; the deck's arrow keys still work while it plays. Cut: upload → parameters → render → download.]**

**Tanya (over the video):** Drag in the sample data. Pick the farmer, pick the year, pick the format. Hit render. That's `{soils}` doing the work underneath, the same functions Jadey showed you. Preview on the right. Download the PDF. That's the whole workflow for a field agent.

The important thing isn't that this is a Shiny app. It's that the person using it never has to know there's a package, a template, or Quarto underneath. They open the bag and eat the cookie.

**[hand-off to Jadey on the next slide]**

`PLACEHOLDER · USER QUOTE / PHOTO`: one real user, one sentence, or a photo of an extension / technical-assistance user with the app.

**Jadey:** Watching people use the app for the first time was the most useful hour of the project. Not because it went smoothly. Because of where it didn't. As the package maintainer, every place a user got stuck was a place `{soils}` had a gap I couldn't see from inside my own kitchen.

**Jadey (land on the line):** The app worked. It also showed us exactly where the package was thin. **[→ Lessons Learned]**
